correctness.rationale: For \(n\ge3\), \(2\le k<n\) and \(0<r<1/2\), cyclic normalized spacings anchored at a uniformly chosen sampled point are uniform on the \((n-1)\)-simplex. Two boundary gaps exceeding \(r\) and \(k-1\) internal gaps at most \(r\) exactly define a proper size-\(k\) component. Translating boundaries then applying inclusion-exclusion gives the formula for \(p_{n,k}\). Convex Minkowski interpolation of the relevant slices and Brunn–Minkowski prove concavity of \(p_{n,k}^{1/(n-1)}\). Endpoint zeros and a Vandermonde non-plateau argument give a unique finite optimizer. For fixed \(k\), compact-uniform convergence to \(e^{-2c}(1-e^{-c})^{k-1}\) and the bounds \(p_{n,k}(c/n)\le c^{k-1}\) and \(p_{n,k}(c/n)\le e^{-c/2}\) yield the optimal scaled radius \(c=\log((k+1)/2)\). All normalization and boundary hypotheses are checked analytically; finite computations do not replace the proof.

originality.rationale: The claimed new statement is global \((n-1)\)-root concavity for each fixed-\(n\) size-\(k\) expected component-count profile, uniqueness of its maximizing radius and sharp asymptotic location \(\log((k+1)/2)/n\). The earlier Huillet joint gap identities cover the raw exact mean, which is expressly excluded from novelty. Decreusefond–Ferraz cover total Poisson cluster counts, and Penrose–Yang address different component-count asymptotic regimes. The inspected source statements do not supply the global power-concavity and optimum theorem without additional convex-slice reasoning. Historical implicit coverage remains a genuine risk.

value.rationale: For geometric network models, the expected number of communities with a prescribed nontrivial vertex count first grows then shrinks as connection radius changes; a piecewise alternating formula does not make a single global peak obvious. The theorem proves a complete finite-sample shape classification and identifies the unique optimal communication scale \(\log((k+1)/2)/n\) for each fixed \(k\). It supplies a natural, motivated size-dependent optimization law beyond recomputation of classical gap-count distributions.
